implementation_notes: The classic roles map one-to-one onto the Collections Framework: a collection implements Iterable (the aggregate creation operation), iterator() returns a java.util.Iterator whose hasNext()/next() are the traversal protocol, and the enhanced for loop desugars to that pair, so clients never see the storage. Implement Iterator directly only when the traversal has no natural backing collection (custom streams, stateful filters) or must be pulled lazily; otherwise implement Iterable and let for-each or forEachRemaining drive it, with fail-fast ConcurrentModificationException on structural modification during iteration.
pitfalls: remove() is an optional operation: it throws UnsupportedOperationException on unmodifiable or immutable sources, and IllegalStateException when called before next() or twice after it.

Structural modification during iteration (changing the collection instead of using the iterator) trips a best-effort fail-fast ConcurrentModificationException - not a guarantee, so a missed detection means silently wrong traversal.

Iterator state is single-pass and not thread-safe; sharing one across threads requires external synchronisation, while the concurrent collections' iterators are weakly consistent and never throw but may or may not see concurrent updates.

variants.name: Stream and Spliterator pipelines
variants.idiom_name: Stream aggregate operations driven by a terminal op; Spliterator as the traversal engine
variants.implementation_notes: Java 8 moves traversal into a declarative pipeline: a Stream describes its source and the aggregate operations (filter/map/reduce) that run when a terminal operation is invoked, and Spliterator is the engine under it - the parallel analogue of Iterator with bulk forEachRemaining, trySplit() for partitioning and lower per-element overhead because it avoids the hasNext/next race. BaseStream.iterator()/spliterator() are the documented escape hatches back to a client-controlled traversal. Choose streams for filtering/aggregation and keep Iterator for stateful, resumable or inherently sequential cursors.
variants.code_sketch:
var total = inventory.stream()
        .filter(Item::isPending)
        .mapToInt(Item::amount)
        .sum();                                   // terminal op drives it
Iterator<Item> back = inventory.stream().iterator();   // documented escape hatch
pitfalls: A stream is consumed by its terminal operation: reusing the variable afterwards throws IllegalStateException, and streams holding a resource (files, IO) need try-with-resources.
Parallel streams split through the Spliterator: a poorly splittable source gains nothing or produces non-deterministic results, and stateful lambdas (mutable accumulators) are unsafe.
Iterator/Spliterator obtained from an in-flight stream are escape hatches with weak consistency guarantees and inherit the stream's single-use semantics.
